query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

The boride layer (BL) formed on the steel surface by boriding treatment can significantly improve its surface properties [,,]. The principal elements in CoCrFeNiMn HEA, such as Fe, Co, and Cr, have a strong tendency to form stable borides [,]. In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). decision.trend: Research has been focused on improving the corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) through various methods such as boronizing, laser cladding, and alloying with different elements. The trend shows that these methods can improve the surface hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of HEAs. However, the corrosion behavior of HEAs in molten aluminum is still a concern.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to improve the resistance of boride-based components to molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment. The current research has not specifically addressed this issue, and the development of a single intervention that can improve the corrosion resistance of boride-based components in this specific application is still needed.
decision.why: Boronizing has been shown to improve the surface hardness and wear resistance of HEAs, and it may also improve the corrosion resistance of boride-based components in molten aluminum. This method involves the diffusion of boron into the surface of the component, forming a boride layer that can provide a barrier against corrosion. The application of boronizing to boride-based components could be a promising approach to improve their corrosion resistance in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
